items.titleEn: Biggest Inn Town on the Road
items.bodyEn: Miya, named for Atsuta Shrine beside it, was the largest post town on the Tōkaidō. The shogunate's 1843 survey counted 248 hatago inns and more than ten thousand residents. Three highways met here, and travelers waited for wind and tide, because the next stage to Kuwana was not walked but sailed.
items.sourceNote: 東海道宿村大概帳 (1843): Miya-juku, 248 hatago, 10,342 residents; Hiroshige, 宮 熱田神事

items.bodyEn: Hiroshige's print for Miya shows no inns, only a festival: two teams of men in matching coats race horses past a torii by torchlight. Atsuta Shrine, which gave the town its name, is among the most venerated in Japan; tradition holds it enshrines Kusanagi, the sword of the imperial regalia. Travelers prayed here before the sea crossing.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Tōkaidō gojūsan-tsugi (Hōeidō ed.), 'Miya: Atsuta Shrine Festival'

items.bodyEn: The 越 of 〜に越したことはない means to cross or to surpass. The Shuowen Jiezi, China's oldest character dictionary, glosses it 'to pass over' and builds it from 走, run, with 戉, an axe, lending only its sound. Japanese keeps both senses in one verb, 越す: you cross a pass, you beat a forecast, and nothing surpasses the best option.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字, c. 100 CE), entry 越: 度也, 从走戉聲

items.titleEn: のみ, the Formal だけ
items.bodyEn: 〜のみならず means 'not only ... but also.' Its core, のみ, is the classical particle for 'only' that survives in formal writing: 会員のみ, members only. In conversation the same idea is 〜だけでなく. Reach for のみならず in essays, reports and speeches, where it signals a written register; among friends it sounds stiff, like saying 'moreover' at dinner.
